etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English sellen, from Old English sellan (“give; give up for money”), from Proto-West Germanic *salljan, from Proto-Germanic *saljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *selh₁-. Compare Danish sælge, Swedish sälja, Icelandic selja.

definitions.definition: (transitive, ditransitive, intransitive) To transfer goods or provide services in exchange for money.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 19:21:
quote.text: If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor.

quote.citation: 2013 August 10, “A new prescription”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8848:
quote.text: No sooner has a [synthetic] drug been blacklisted than chemists adjust their recipe and start churning out a subtly different one. These “legal highs” are sold for the few months it takes the authorities to identify and ban them, and then the cycle begins again.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To promote (a product or service) although not being paid in any direct way or at all.

quote.citation: 2016, “The Fetal Kick Catalyst”, in The Big Bang Theory:
quote.text: Howard: You're gonna feel terrible when I'm in a wheelchair. Which, by the way, would fit easily in the back of this award-winning minivan.Bernadette: Fine, we'll go to the E.R. Just stop selling me on the van.Howard: You're right. It sells itself.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To betray for money or other things.
(transitive, slang) To trick, cheat, or manipulate someone.

quote.citation: 1605 (first performance), Ben[jamin] Jonson, Ben: Ionson His Volpone or The Foxe, [London]:  […]  [George Eld] for Thomas Thorppe, published 1607, →OCLC, (please specify the Internet Archive page):
quote.text: Then weaues Other crosse-plots New tricks for safety, are sought; They thriue: When, bold, Each tempt's th'other againe, and all are sold.

quote.citation: 1884, Mark Twain, chapter XXIII, in The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn:
quote.text: House was jammed again that night, and we sold this crowd the same way.

quote.citation: 2011 January 12, Saj Chowdhury, “Blackpool 2-1 Liverpool”, in BBC:
quote.text: Raul Meireles was the victim of the home side's hustling on this occasion giving the ball away to the impressive David Vaughan who slipped in Taylor-Fletcher. The striker sold Daniel Agger with the best dummy of the night before placing his shot past keeper Pepe Reina.

definitions.definition: (transitive, professional wrestling, slang) To pretend that an opponent's blows or maneuvers are causing legitimate injury; to act.
(Australia, slang, intransitive) To throw under the bus; to let down one's own team in an endeavour, especially in a sport or a game.

quote.citation: 1963, American Society of Travel Agents, ASTA Travel News, volume 32, page 55:
quote.text: Now the easiest sell in traveldom is made even easier.

definitions.definition: (figurative, by extension) The promotion of an idea for acceptance.
(colloquial, dated) An imposition, a cheat; a hoax; a disappointment; anything occasioning a loss of pride or dignity.

quote.citation: 1919, W[illiam] Somerset Maugham, “chapter 12”, in The Moon and Sixpence, [New York, N.Y.]: Grosset & Dunlap Publishers […], →OCLC:
quote.text: "Of course a miracle may happen, and you may be a great painter, but you must confess the chances are a million to one against it. It'll be an awful sell if at the end you have to acknowledge you've made a hash of it."

quote.citation: 1922, Katherine Mansfield, The Doll's House (Selected Stories, Oxford World's Classics paperback 2002, 354)

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French selle, from Latin sella.

quote.citation: 1600, [Torquato Tasso], “The Fourth Booke of Godfrey of Bulloigne”, in Edward Fairefax [i.e., Edward Fairfax], transl., Godfrey of Bulloigne, or The Recouerie of Ierusalem. […], London:  […]  Ar[nold] Hatfield, for I[saac] Iaggard and M[atthew] Lownes, →OCLC, stanza 7, page 56:
quote.text: The tyrant proud frown’d from his loftie cell, [...].

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto II”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: turning to that place, in which whyleare / He left his loftie steed with golden sell, / And goodly gorgeous barbes, him found not theare [...].

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old Saxon seill or Old Norse seil. Cognate with Dutch zeel (“rope”), German Seil (“rope”).

definitions.definition: (regional, obsolete) A rope (usually for tying up cattle, but can also mean any sort of rope).
